world_behind.title: Four hundred and seventy years of monarchy
world_behind.text: The Nephites have been ruled by kings since Nephi was made one against his own objection, and every book in this record so far is dated by a reign. The last verse of the chapter closes that whole institution, and the arithmetic two verses earlier counts five hundred and nine years since Lehi left Jerusalem.

world_behind.title: No new legislation anywhere in the reform
world_behind.text: Verse 25 sends them to the laws given by the fathers, called correct and given by the hand of the Lord. What changes is who applies those laws and whose head the failures land on. A constitution is replaced without a statute being written.

world_behind.title: The analysis of tyranny is written by a monarch
world_behind.text: Verses 21 through 23 are a practical account of how a bad king keeps his throne, and the man setting it out is a good king describing the trade he is in. Nothing in the passage is hypothetical to him; he names his own predecessor two verses earlier.

world_behind.title: Review in two directions
world_behind.text: Judges who do not judge by the law can be brought before a higher judge. Higher judges who fail can be judged by a small number of lower judges, by the voice of the people. The chapter builds an appeal upward and an appeal downward and gives each one verse.

world_behind.title: A borrowed sentence
world_behind.text: "If it were possible that you could have just men to be your kings" is very nearly what Alma said at Helam six chapters earlier when his own people wanted to crown him. Two men decline power with the same concession, and the record puts both refusals on the page without connecting them.

world_behind.title: The book closes on arithmetic
world_behind.text: Mosiah dies at sixty-three in the thirty-third year of his reign, five hundred and nine years after Lehi left Jerusalem. Alma dies at eighty-two. The last sentence of the book is an obituary.

words.text: A stepping-in between two parties, the act of placing oneself in a gap. The verse credits it to the all-wise Creator and pairs it with the people's sincere repentance. Without it, the verse says, they must unavoidably have remained in bondage until now.

To remove from a throne. The word appears once in scripture, and Mosiah uses it to make a practical point: you cannot do it without much contention and the shedding of much blood. The argument against kings here is partly about the cost of removing a bad one.

Makes into law. The verb is legislative and the record uses it of an unrighteous king issuing laws after the manner of his own wickedness. What makes him dangerous in this description is the ability to make his wickedness lawful.

Contrary to, in conflict with. This is the older legal sense rather than the modern sense of disgusting. The things a bad king does are described as expressly repugnant to the commandments of God, which frames them as a clash of statutes.

Gave up a claim voluntarily. The people relinquished their desires for a king, a change they surrendered themselves. The same verse has them becoming anxious that every man should have an equal chance.

Money, with the taint of corrupt gain attached. It occurs once more in this record and several times in Paul's letters about who may hold office. It also names what Samuel's sons turned aside after, the failure of judges that made Israel demand a king in the first place.

phrases.term: He to whom the kingdom doth rightly belong has declined
phrases.text: The whole crisis in one clause, and it is stated as a fact about a person. Mosiah does not argue that monarchy is wrong here. He begins by reporting that the legitimate heir will not serve.

phrases.term: Let us appoint judges, to judge this people according to our law
phrases.text: The proposal, and the first person plural is doing work. He does not decree it; he proposes it and keeps the throne for the remainder of his days while the transition happens. The judges are to judge by a law that already exists.

phrases.term: Because all men are not just it is not expedient that ye should have a king
phrases.text: The whole argument, and it turns on a fact about people rather than about institutions. Verse 13 has already granted that just kings would be preferable. The case against monarchy is built entirely on the unreliability of the supply.

phrases.term: He has his friends in iniquity, and he keepeth his guards about him
phrases.text: Two mechanisms named before any of the laws are mentioned: a network and a bodyguard. The phrase occurs once in scripture. What makes a bad king hard to remove, in this account, is other people.

phrases.term: It is common for the lesser part of the people to desire that which is not right
phrases.text: The premise underneath majority rule, stated with unusual care. It is not that the many are good; it is that the wrong is more commonly the minority position. The clause appears once in scripture and the sentence after it makes the observation into law.

phrases.term: They shall be answered upon their own heads
phrases.text: The moral center of the reform. Under kings, verse 31 says, the people's sins were answered upon the heads of their kings. Under judges, each person carries his own. The phrase occurs once in scripture, and verse 38 has the people accepting the arrangement explicitly.

phrases.term: Every man might bear his part
phrases.text: Government described as weight rather than as authority. The verse before has Mosiah unfolding the trials, troubles, and travails of soul that come with the office, and this is his conclusion: it ought not to sit on one man. The phrase is unique in scripture.

phrases.term: Thus ended the reign of the kings over the people of Nephi
phrases.text: The last sentence of the book, and it is paired with the death of the man who founded the church. Four hundred and seventy years of Nephite monarchy close in half a verse, and the other half belongs to Alma.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: A poll, and a written answer
verses.text: He asks the country who should be king. The voice names Aaron, who is gone and unwilling, as are his brothers. So the king sends a second message, and this one is written down.

verses.label: v. 5–10
verses.title: The case against appointing anyone
verses.text: If someone else is installed, the rightful heir might come back angry, draw away a part of the people, and cause wars. Nobody has the right to destroy either man to prevent it. The argument is entirely about what could go wrong later.

verses.label: v. 11–16
verses.title: Judges instead, and the reason
verses.text: He will finish his own reign and then judges will be appointed to judge by the existing law. Verse 13 concedes that consistently just kings would be fine, naming his father as the example. Verse 16 supplies the objection: not all men are just.

verses.label: v. 17–24
verses.title: How a bad king holds on
verses.text: Noah is named. Then the mechanism: friends, guards, the laws of righteous predecessors torn up, new ones enacted after his own wickedness, dissenters destroyed, armies sent. And a note that removing such a man costs blood.

verses.label: v. 25–31
verses.title: The rule, and the appeal
verses.text: Choose judges by the voice of the people; do your business that way; and if judges fail, there is review in both directions. Then the reason it matters: sins answered upon their own heads instead of upon a king's.

verses.label: v. 32–38
verses.title: Liberty, and the transfer of guilt
verses.text: A land of liberty, every man enjoying his rights and privileges alike, the burden of government shared out. He explains the trials of a righteous king and the disadvantages of an unrighteous one, and the people give up wanting a king and accept answering for themselves.

verses.label: v. 40–47
verses.title: Two obituaries, and a new clock
verses.text: They loved him because he had not exacted riches or delighted in blood. Judges are appointed; Alma is the first, and also the high priest. Then the dates: sixty- three years, thirty-three of them reigning, five hundred and nine since Jerusalem.

chapter.title: The reform starts from an accident, not a principle
chapter.text: The people voted for Aaron. Aaron was in Lamanite country and would not come back for it. The argument, the judges, the voice of the people as law: everything that follows proceeds from a vacancy that nobody designed.

chapter.title: The case is made in writing, and reading is what persuades
chapter.text: The king circulates a document instead of convening an assembly, and verse 37 says that after he sent these things forth the people were convinced. In a record full of sermons, the decisive speech is one nobody heard delivered.

chapter.title: The argument concedes the other side first
chapter.text: Just kings would be preferable, and his own father was one. Only then: not all men are just. The concession is the same one Alma made at Helam when his people offered him a crown, in nearly the same words.

chapter.title: The moral core is transferred liability
chapter.text: Under kings, a people's sins are answered on the king's head; under judges, on their own. Mosiah states it at verse 30, repeats the mechanism at 31, and verse 38 has the people expressing willingness to answer for their own sins. The reform is described as a redistribution of guilt before it is described as a redistribution of power.

chapter.title: The waters of Mormon covenant, scaled to a nation
chapter.text: Alma's congregation had promised to bear one another's burdens. Here the burden is the government itself, and every man is to bear his part. The same figure runs from a spring in the wilderness to a constitution.

chapter.title: The risk is named at the moment of adoption
chapter.text: Verse 27: if the time comes that the voice of the people chooses iniquity, the judgments of God will come. Nothing in the chapter claims that majorities are reliable, only that minorities are more often wrong.

chapter.title: Two offices land on one man
chapter.text: The chapter separates the crown from the judiciary and then makes Alma both chief judge and high priest. It reports this without remark, in the same verse that says his father conferred the church on him.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: Mosiah 28 emptied the throne; this chapter replaces it. The dating system changes with it. From here the record counts years by the reign of the judges. The book ends with the monarchy and the founder of the church closing in the same sentence.

applications.title: Concede the strong version first
applications.text: He granted that good kings would be better than judges, and named one, before arguing that you cannot count on getting them. An argument that will not admit the best case against it is not usually believed.

applications.title: Argue about who is actually available
applications.text: The objection is that just men are not reliably available. When judging a system, ask what it does with the people you will actually get rather than the people you would like.

applications.title: Put it in writing when it matters
applications.text: He wrote the case out and sent it around, and they were convinced after reading. Written arguments can be reread, checked, and considered without the arguer in the room.

applications.title: Ask who absorbs the consequences
applications.text: The reform's real content is that people started answering for their own sins. In any arrangement you are part of, work out whose head the failures land on.

applications.title: Share the work of governing
applications.text: The instruction is that every man bear his part of governing. Sharing the work is the version of shared responsibility that actually costs something.

applications.title: Name the risk while you are adopting the thing
applications.text: He installed majority rule and said in the same breath what would happen if the majority chose wrongly. Adopting something without stating its failure mode is how the failure mode gets forgotten.

applications.title: Notice how a bad leader actually holds on
applications.text: Friends in iniquity and guards: a network and protection, named before any mention of laws or armies. Power is usually held in place by people.

questions.text: What am I holding onto that rightly belongs to someone who has declined it?
Where am I arguing for a system that only works with ideal people in it?
Whose friendship is making something wrong easier to sustain?
Whose head do my failures currently land on?
What part of a shared burden am I letting somebody else carry?
What would I have to give up to have an equal chance be general rather than mine?
